items.q: In the relational model, a row and a column are, respectively:
options: One record (e.g. one user) and one field (e.g. email)

explain.right: A table's row is a single record; a column is a single typed field shared by every row.
explain.wrong: Databases, queries, indexes, and keys are different concepts; a row is a record and a column is a field.

options: A duplicate copy of the whole related row
A column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table, linking them
A key that only works in another country's servers

explain.right: A foreign key stores another table's primary-key value to relate the two, so data is referenced once rather than copied.
explain.wrong: It isn't a password or a duplicate of the row; the point is to link by reference, not to copy.

items.q: What does adding an index to a column do?
options: Builds a sorted lookup structure so matching rows are found in ~O(log n) instead of scanning every row, at the cost of space and slower writes
Guarantees every query is instant with no downsides
Makes an exact copy of the whole table

explain.right: An index (often a B-tree) lets the database jump to matching rows (~O(log n)) instead of an O(n) scan, paying extra storage and slower writes.
explain.wrong: It isn't a copy of the table, it isn't free of downsides, and it doesn't deduplicate rows.

items.q: A bank transfer debits account A and credits account B inside one transaction. What does this guarantee?
options: Both happen or neither does — they succeed or fail as one unit (atomicity)
The money moves twice to be safe
Other users always see the half-finished transfer
The debit happens even if the credit fails

explain.right: A transaction is all-or-nothing (atomicity): a failure mid-way rolls back, so you never end up debited-but-not-credited.
explain.wrong: It never leaves the debit without the credit, doesn't move money twice, and isolation hides half-done work from others.

items.q: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Pick two and explain what each promises in plain words.
rubric: Atomicity: all operations in a transaction happen or none do (roll back on failure)
Consistency: the database goes from one valid state to another, with constraints (keys/types) still holding
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work, as if run one at a time
Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes/power loss

explain.right: Any two correctly explained: all-or-nothing (A), valid-to-valid state (C), concurrent transactions don't interfere (I), committed data survives a crash (D).
explain.wrong: A weak answer just expands the letters without saying what each actually promises, or confuses isolation with atomicity.
